items.title: Fable 5.1 didn't come with document OCR benchmarks, so we benchmarked it on ParseBench: a comprehens...
items.content:
Fable 5.1 didn't come with document OCR benchmarks, so we benchmarked it on ParseBench: a comprehensive parsing benchmark that's comprised of 2k+ real-world documents across finance, legal, insurance, and more.

As a positive note, it is one of the first frontier models in recent memory where document OCR performance actually improved between model generations! 
✅ It beats Fable 5 across the board on all of our metrics, from tables/content faithfulness/formatting/charts/visual grounding
✅ It is one of the best models out there for parsing tables

This is great, because while frontier models have rapidly advanced on reasoning benchmarks, they have not advanced on visual understanding. Prior to this the latest models (Opus 5, 5.6-Sol, 3.7 Flash) have stagnated on visual understanding tasks. 

Obviously you shouldn't use Fable 5.1 as a document OCR tool on its own; besides missing needed metadata, it also costs 15c a page - which is 10-15x more expensive than our default agentic mode on LlamaParse (which performs similarly). 

If you're interested in tracking the 90+ solutions that we've benchmarked on doc OCR, check out ParseBench: https://t.co/PWczfhosZp

If you're looking for a dedicated, SOTA OCR tool to power your doc processing workloads, check out LlamaParse: https://t.co/XYZmx5T7JA

items.title:
If your agent executes code, you want to run it in an isolated environment.

I learned this the hard...
items.content:
If your agent executes code, you want to run it in an isolated environment.

I learned this the hard way.

I also know a couple of people who let OpenClaw go nuts and had to wipe out their laptops after a few days to clean up the mess.

Two rules you must always follow:

1. Agent that runs code → isolated environment
2. Agent that controls a browser → isolated environment

But that generates a new problem: that environment has to start quickly, use as little memory as possible, and give you enough control to operate it.

This is hard to achieve, but you don't need to reinvent the wheel:

Cube Sandbox is an open-source MicroVM sandbox developed by Tencent Cloud. Think of it as a production-grade agent infrastructure that you can use to run agents at scale.

Cube Sandbox uses RustVMM and KVM to run each sandbox with hardware-level isolation.

• It cold-starts in under 60ms
• It uses less than 5MB of RAM overhead
• You can launch tens of thousands of sandboxes within a minute

Here is what you can do with it:

1. Capture, clone, and restore sandbox state with snapshots and rollback
2. Deploy sandbox clusters through Kubernetes
3. Run workloads on ARM infrastructure
4. Observe what happens inside agent executions
5. Govern ingress and egress traffic
6. Persistent volumes and cross-machine pause/resume

Here is the GitHub repository:
https://t.co/2X3k2NQEE8

You can inspect the code and try it out with your own agent workflow.

items.content:
Two years ago, people would scream at you if you said that writing code was obsolete.

Today, most people agree: writing code is no longer viable.

Now, we are living through the same exact cycle with "reading code".

In a year or two, you won't be manually reading AI-generated code anymore.

Code = low-bandwidth

Reviewing code is doable when:

• You wrote it
• You have a manageable amount of it

Reviewing code is not doable when:

• You didn't write it
• You have tons of it

We are quickly moving towards "infinite, ~free automatically generated code". It's crazy to think you'll still be reading every line of code in a year or two.

Tons of people who want to learn computer vision don't know what to build to start learning.

Here is a really good opportunity to jump right into the deep end:

Amazon Developers is running a virtual hackathon. You can participate solo or with a team, and there are $190,000 in prizes.

The Ring track focuses on building with Amazon computer vision APIs, which is gold for anyone who wants to work with cameras and computer vision.

Here are a few ideas:

1. Build a package delivery detector that identifies when a package is left at the door and sends a notification with a snapshot.

2. Recognize when your dog is waiting by the door and notify you that it wants to come inside.

3. Count how many people enter and leave your office or studio on any given day.

4. Use the camera to detect whether the garage door is open and alert you if it stays open too long.

You have 8 weeks to build a working demo.

Best case, you'll win some prize money. Worst case, you'll learn a ton and have a pretty cool demo to show during interviews.

Here is what I can tell you:

Getting your hands dirty and building something here is 10x better than watching another tutorial.

items.title: Diffusion models somehow learn to produce new images from finite datasets even though a naïve high-d...
items.content:
Diffusion models somehow learn to produce new images from finite datasets even though a naïve high-dimensional model should need vastly more examples as image size grows, while an exact model that simply reasons over the whole training set tends to end up reproducing training images.

In this recent paper from @Stanford, he authors try to understand what separates these two behaviors. They introduce BIRD models, a simplified family of diffusion models in which each pixel is allowed to use only part of the noisy image and then performs Bayesian inference—assigning probabilities to which training examples could have produced what it sees—to decide how to denoise that pixel.

This setup leads to the following discovery: there is a sharp boundary between memorization and generalization determined by mutual information, meaning how much observing the restricted noisy image tells the model about the original image; when that information exceeds the logarithm of the number of training examples, the model can identify individual examples and memorizes, while below it many examples remain plausible and the model generalizes.

Read this paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/dSPCrd8HO5

I went from 50kg to 80kg so added 30kg in weight and now cutting back to 70kg

Point is, don't believe everything you see on the internet!

A healthy natural fit body is unimpressive in a world of people on gear (which is fine too btw but not for me or him)
